result:
If I could change one thing, I'd make people *much* better at updating their beliefs when confronted with evidence.

Not smarter in the raw IQ sense, and not more "empathetic" in the vague feel-good way. Just dramatically less attached to being wrong. A built-in resistance to motivated reasoning, tribal loyalty over facts, and the usual human habit of bending reality to fit what we already want to believe.

Most of the world's biggest problems—bad policies, pointless conflicts, technological stagnation, even personal misery—aren't primarily caused by lack of resources or intelligence. They're caused by people refusing to see what's in front of them because it threatens their identity, status, or narrative. Fix that cognitive failure mode and a lot of other things start solving themselves.

Everything else (poverty, disease, conflict, even existential risk) becomes much more tractable when the default human response to new information is "maybe I'm wrong, let's check" instead of "how do I defend my position?"

It's not a flashy answer, but it feels like the highest-leverage single change. Most other utopian tweaks either require constant enforcement or create new problems downstream. This one would compound over time.
